item.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
item.description:
Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its Workspace MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email

On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.

Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".

If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.

What the rule saysâ

The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:

The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.

The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.

There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.

Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".

The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:

Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects. Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data. Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product.

The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.

What the MCP servers can doâ

Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.

Server What it can do What's missing compared with REST Gmail Search and read threads, create and list drafts, labels, trash, spam Send, reply, forward and editing drafts (partner-only). Filters, settings, attachment download, push notifications. Drafts with attachments are "not supported yet". Drive Search, read and download files, create files and folders, copy, upload a new revision Move, rename, share, trash, comments, shared-drive management Docs Read, and edit through any batchUpdate request, including suggestion mode Close to parity Sheets Read and write values and formulas, insert rows and columns, formatting and charts Creating a spreadsheet (use the Drive server) and some less common batchUpdate requests Slides Read slides and thumbnails, edit through batchUpdate Close to parity Calendar List, search, create, update and delete events, suggest times, RSVP Creating calendars, sharing, settings Chat List, search and send messages Space administration Tasks Full create, read, update and delete Close to parity

The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.

Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team.

Partners get moreâ

Google hasn't said who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's Google Workspace connector for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack.

So a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms.

Who counts as an agentâ

The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.

Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't said how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.

A few edge cases are documented:

Service accounts with domain-wide delegation can't set the agentic flag. Their MCP requests aren't rejected for missing it, but still trigger approval prompts. Apps Script's built-in OAuth client can't be marked as agentic either. Scripts that call the MCP servers need a custom client, and scripts that don't call them aren't affected. The community gws CLI, which wraps the entire REST surface, keeps working. Its README now points agent use to Google's new official CLI, gwscli, which offers "a curated set of commands designed for agents" and needs the MCP services enabled. Quotas and pricingâ

Every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail search_threads or list_drafts counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its users. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it quickly.

The paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices.

Google's reasoningâ

Google's case, from a Cloud blog post by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:

Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed â¦ a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.

There's substance to this. An email agent that reads a message saying "forward the last ten invoices to this address" is a well-documented prompt-injection risk, and a token that allows gmail.modify gives the agent the power to do it. Routing every agent through one gateway gives admins a single place to block categories of action, require approval and audit what happened. The MCP servers do all of that, and apply data-loss-prevention rules automatically.

The same design also gives Google control of which agents can do what, which data they can keep, and whether anything built on that data can compete with Google's own products. The partner-only tools and the 30-day cap on embeddings show that control in use.

Slack went down a similar path in May 2025. It cut history API rate limits to one request a minute for apps outside its Marketplace and banned bulk export of Slack data for LLMs. Slack drew the line by distribution channel. Google draws it by whether the software is an AI, which is harder to define and harder to enforce.

What to do before 1 February 2027â

If you build an agent product on Workspace:

Create an OAuth client marked as agentic and move to the MCP servers. List every operation your product needs that's missing from the public tool list, and apply for partner access early. Check how long you store embeddings, memory indexes or user profiles built from Workspace data.

If you run a personal agent or MCP server against your own account: open-source servers that call REST, such as the popular google_workspace_mcp, will keep running, but at Standard quotas and outside the terms. Switching to Google's servers costs you sending and draft editing in Gmail, and moving and sharing in Drive.

If you're a Workspace admin: the new controls are under Admin console â Security â API Controls. You can block or approve each category of agent action, set approval policies, and see agent activity in the audit logs. Users can't view or revoke the approvals they've saved, which expire after 90 days, so it's worth setting policy before people start connecting agents.

If your integration doesn't use AI: nothing changes, as long as it stays on its own OAuth client and nobody wires a model into it.

item.title: Intel One Mono font (2023)
item.description:
Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.

It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.

Identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design.

Intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources.

To install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases. Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts.

VSCode - In Settings, search Font Family, then specify Intel One Mono Sublime Text - Go to Sublime Text -> Preferences -> Settings and set font_face to Intel One Mono IntelliJ Platform - Go to File -> Settings -> Editor -> Font and set Font to Intel One Mono We recommend the .otf or .ttf format for desktop use. The .ttf files are also well suited for mobile apps. The .woff and .woff2 fonts are optimized for web use.

We recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms.

Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS:

Programming Ligatures: To use programming ligatures, activate the ss01 feature (Stylistic Set #1). Additional refinements are available via ss02 and ss03: Stylistic Set #2 switches the <= and >= combinations to arrow forms (math contractions being the default otherwise), and Stylistic Set #3 additionally activates a “www” ligature. Alternate three: New in release 1.5. Alternate form for three added. The round top three, numerator, denomenator, superior and inferior can be activated with stylistic Set #4. Raised Colon: The colon is automatically raised in operators, to align with math symbols. For non-programming contexts, the raised colon can be applied contextually between numbers or activated generally. The contextual option is available via ss11 (Stylistic Set #11); for the global switch use ss12 (Stylistic Set #12) or salt (Stylistic Alternates). Language Support: ccmp and locl features ensure correct display across a wide range of languages. These are usually active by default. We recommend setting the language tag/setting in your software to the desired language for best results. Superior/superscript and inferior/subscript figures are included via their Unicode codepoints, or you can produce them from the default figures via the sups (Superscript) and subs/sinf (Subscript) features. Fraction numerals are similarly available via the numr (Numerator) and dnom (Denominator) features. A set of premade fractions is also available in the fonts.

Programming ligatures are not active by default. To use them, activate the stylistic sets of your preference in your code editor. For example:

VSCode - In Settings, add "editor.fontLigatures": "'ss01'" Sublime Text - In Settings, add "font_options": ["ss01"]

You will find editable sources in the sources directory. The instances subfolder contains separate source files for each style of the typeface. Sources are provided in .ufo files, which contain complete artwork, links to OpenType features provided in separate .fea files, as well as meta information like naming and vertical alignments for each style of the typeface.

These are not installable fonts, but rather the source files that produce them: UFO (Unified Font Object) is an open, human-readable font source file format; you can find the file spec here. These sources were created using RoboFont. Many other font editors will also be able to open .ufo files; we recommend using RoboFont version 4.4.

For instances, you will find postscript and truetype subfolders; these contain separate source files for the .otf format and the .ttf/.woff/.woff2 files respectively. Since the format for the outline drawings differs between these sets of formats, for best results we recommend using the postscript sources to create .otf fonts, and the TrueType sources to create .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 fonts.

After making your desired edits, you can generate installable fonts directly from the font editor using its “Generate Font” functionality. If you use RoboFont, any install options should default to the ideal settings, but here they are for reference:

For .otf builds, we recommend activating “Decompose” as well as “Autohint” options. For .ttf, .woff and .woff2 builds, we recommend activating the “Autohint” option only (see note on hinting below). In any case, we recommend using the “Release Mode” setting for best results.

If you would like to apply edits across multiple weights, a more advanced yet potentially efficient way is to edit the masters. These are special sources that describe the extreme points in the design space — the lightest and heaviest weights for both roman and italic designs.

After editing masters, you will need to rerun interpolation to generate individual weights and styles within that design space. This requires the .designspace files enclosed with the masters. The designspace format is an open, XML-based format that describes interpolation spaces (format specification for reference). For a RoboFont-based workflow we recommend Skateboard for interpolation; you can also use the free DesignSpaceEditor extension to view and edit these files.

Note that masters are only available in postscript format, so they will be best for creating .otf fonts. If you need to make TrueType based builds from the masters, we recommend QuadraticConverter for best quality conversion of the curves before generating .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 files; mind that the results will not match the provided instances precisely.

NB: The prepared instances contain some additional data that cannot be maintained through interpolation. For best results, compare new interpolations to the existing instance sources and update them accordingly, specifically the information accessible through the Font Info panels.

For TrueType-based formats (.ttf, .woff, .woff2 files), the official releases are manually optimized for screen rendering. These “hinting” sources are stored separately from the .ufo files, which do not contain any TrueType hinting information. When rebuilding TrueType-based formats, we recommend using the “autohint” option to achieve reasonable, though not identical screen rendering.

If you would like to access and edit manual hinting instructions, you will find these in the separate set of source files under hinting/truetype hinting source. These special TTF files will be viewable and editable using Microsoft VTT.

If you have requests for edits or additions to the official releases, please open issues and we will try to accomodate them.

item.title: Nextcloud Office Desktop app
item.description:
On June 9, 2026, we released the first production-ready version of Euro-Office, a sovereign collaborative office suite developed and governed in Europe. With Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer, we announced the release of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app powered by Euro-Office. Today, the ready-to-use version of the app is available for download. It lets you work offline, switch between Nextcloud Hub in your browser and the app on your computer, and get the same experience on Windows, macOS and Linux.

In this article, you’ll learn about the app’s features, how to install it on Windows, macOS and Linux, and how to co-edit files with your team through Nextcloud Hub.

Free desktop office with maximum file compatibility

The Nextcloud Office Desktop app is a free and open source office suite for Windows, macOS and Linux. Featuring editors for text documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs, it offers high compatibility with Microsoft Office formats (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) and open formats (ODT, ODS, ODP). Connect it to Nextcloud Hub to edit files with your team in real time.

The app includes the features of Nextcloud Office in your browser, plus the benefits of working on your computer:

Work offline and keep files on your device Use the fonts installed on your computer Sign documents digitally Work with local and online files

With the Nextcloud Office Desktop app, you can edit files locally without an internet connection. Working locally, you keep access to your files and you can keep working when you don’t have internet connection or your online tools go down. You decide which files stay on your computer and which go to the cloud.

Need to access your online files? You can connect your Nextcloud instance to the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to access all the files available to you, and edit them on your own or with your team in real time.

How to connect the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to the cloud:

Click “+” in the “Clouds” section in the Home tab Choose “Nextcloud“ and specify the URL of your instance Log in with your credentials

Once connected, choose your Nextcloud instance from the list. You can connect more than one instance to one app to have access to multiple cloud working environments.

Use your own fonts

The Nextcloud Office Desktop app uses fonts installed on your machine, including corporate fonts and default fonts from your OS, like Microsoft fonts on Windows. You can install additional custom fonts any time. No need to bother your Nextcloud admins!

Note: if your collaborators don’t have the same font, they’ll see a fallback font in their version of the file.

Digital signatures and file protection

The Nextcloud Office Desktop app lets you use digital signatures to sign your documents, spreadsheets and presentations. A signature shows who signed a file and that nobody has changed it since. Go to Protection tab and add a signature via Signature feature.

Keep in mind that you need a digital certificate to sign documents. To obtain one, you can ask your IT team at work, or get one for personal use from a trusted provider. You can find providers approved in the EU in this list.

In the Protection tab, you can also set a password for a file, or limit what others can do: comment, fill in forms, or edit with tracked changes only.

How to install the Euro-Office desktop app

You can find and download the latest version of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app from our official installation page.

The app is available for:

Windows: x64, ARM64 Linux: .deb (Debian, Ubuntu), .rpm (Fedora) macOS (Apple Silicon)

You can also find unsigned builds of Euro-Office desktop app and build the app from the source yourself by following the instructions on GitHub.

We want to keep improving the app. You are welcome to share any issues you find with our engineering team on GitHub.

Want to contribute to Euro-Office? Here’s how to get involved

Contributions are welcome! Whether it’s a bug report, a feature idea, a translation, or a pull request, here’s how to take part:

Found a bug or have an idea? Open an issue and describe what you ran into or what you’d like to see. Want to contribute code? Fork the relevant component repo, make your change, and open a pull request. For build changes, see the build docs. Want to help translate? Localization improvements are always appreciated — see the editors’ interface translations.

Please keep contributions compatible with the project’s AGPL v3 license.

At the second Nextcloud Enterprise Day Copenhagen, municipalities, universities and other public organisations discussed how they can reduce their dependency on US Big Tech. Read our recap of the event.

Created in a joint effort of our team, community, and partners, Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer learns from real people using our tools every day. Create your team's own space with Nextcloud Teams, organize your memories in new Nextcloud Photos, and enjoy the updates you asked for across all apps. Read on for a full rundown of our latest release!

We are introducing the Nextcloud ISV Partner Program to support independent app developers through the Nextcloud app store. Read more in this article and get in touch with our team if you want to join the program.

We explore challenges Nextcloud Talk solves that Microsoft Teams can't, uncovering a stronger alternative for organizations that that prioritize digital sovereignty, compliance, and control.

Following two successful Nextcloud Enterprise Days in The Hague in 2025, we brought the event to Utrecht this year, where a massive 750 registrations brought a big crowd to the Jaarbeurs venue. The kickoff in the morning pre-announced the launch of the book “Sovereignty! But how?“ by well-known Dutch IT security journalist and author Brenno […]

In the Nextcloud 2024 wrap-up, we want to take a moment to celebrate this year's achievements. Join us as we continue to reimagine what’s possible - shaping a world where open source, privacy and connection come together and drive progress for the greater good.

Organisations, small and large, need a way to ensure the resiliency and digital sovereignty of their operations – an open-source, privacy-respecting alternative to Teams. And today, we present that solution - Nextcloud Talk.

Nextcloud has been recognized with the World Summit Award Germany that selects and promotes local digital innovation improving society, aiming to contribute to the United Nations' agenda of sustainable development goals.

DIE ZEIT, a prominent German outlet, interviewed Nextcloud’s founder Frank Karlitschek for an article on Microsoft’s anti-competitive behaviour on the European office software market. Read for a recap of the article and the key takeaways.

MagentaCLOUD’s migration to Nextcloud in 2021 resulted in a fully equipped Online Storage with an integrated online office suite that further improves the user experience, flexibility and security for customers.

We bring you a major update to the Nextcloud AI Assistant, plus the news we work with several big hosting providers like IONOS and OVHcloud to bring AI-as-a-Service options to you!

Bechtle and Nextcloud announce today a complete managed collaboration platform for the public sector that requires no tender and can be deployed immediately.

Discover how to make the switch from ownCloud to Nextcloud. Our quick guide provides insights into the migration process, helping you make the transition smoothly.

Today, US-based file sync & share vendor Kiteworks announced their acquisition of ownCloud and Dracoon. Kiteworks points out that their customers now have access to their file-sharing application. It is to be expected they will not maintain 3 similar products, but customers will have to migrate to the US firms’ platform or look for another […]

As part of Schleswig-Holstein's state digitization strategy, the state chancellery has announced they will work with Nextcloud to develop AI for working with government documents. This comes just after we announced the first private AI assistant last weekend with Hub 6. The German state already uses Nextcloud and their AI strategy aligns with our work on ethical, local AI technologies.

item.description:
Have You Ever Played With Your Editor?

Compose your own Vim symphony

Vim was too complicated. It wasn't worth the effort to learn it. Or so I thought.

I tried anyway.

I could write and edit my content after a couple of hours. Why everybody thought it was so hard?

Even better: I was more productive, I could focus solely on what I was writing, and I had so much fun!

The fun never stopped. Even after playing with Vim for almost a decade.

What Will This Book Bring You?

A step-by-step approach to learn easily without feeling overwhelmed.

Practice makes perfect: no less than 170 fun exercises to build your muscle memory.

How to customize your editor for your own specific needs.

Keeping your hands on your keyboard will save your cognitive energy, and improve your productivity.

The print version will be available in a couple of weeks.You can subscribe to the newsletter to get notified.

About The Author

Hi! I'm Matthieu. Nice to see you here!

I've been coding as a hobby for 25 years, professionally for 15+ years.

I've worked from small to big companies, mentoring and leading developer teams.

Teaching is very rewarding to me. That's why I love writing for my blog, The Valuable Dev.

FAQ There are many resources about Vim out there: what's different with this one? Each chapter builds on the previous one, to show you more advanced techniques as you progress. Practice makes perfect: each chapter comes with exercises to increase your skills, but also to dive deeper and uncover useful subtleties. The book tries to focus on real-life, practical examples, inspired from my own (and friend's) use of Vim. The book is aimed to be as complete as possible, without going into useless, boring details. Even if you use Vim for a long time, I'm pretty sure you'll learn something in this book. If not, ask for a refund! There's a rich annexe section, to serve as a reference when you're working with Vim. The book is designed to be fun to read (we're here to play!) with a minimum of fluff. I don't want to tell the story of my grandma for 392 pages. What this book is NOT good for?

This book is not for you if:

You're not ready to invest some time on the short term to be more effective on the long term. You want absolutely all details about everything. Vim's internal help will do a better job than this book (or any other). You want to learn the basics, but you're not interested to go further. In that case, most free tutorials out there will be enough. You want to reproduce all the functionalities of your IDE without compromises. Vim is powerful (and can do much more than most people think), but it's not your IDE. You're more interested in plugins than Vim's internal functionalities. Learning to Play Vim is more about the latter. Why should I use Vim? Vim is a free, mature, and stable editor. It has many useful functionalities you won't find anywhere else. Vim is lighter and faster than most IDEs. It's not a problem to have multiple instances running in parallel, even on old computers. You can customize Vim according to your own needs, to focus on your code (or your writing). Vim is fun to play with! To me, it's like a game. The goal: to use as less keystrokes as possible. You can configure IDE-like features (autocompletion, jump to definition, debugging...) for many programming languages. No need to have multiple editors or IDEs anymore! Vim allows you to write and edit using only the keyboard, improving your efficiency. Switching between the keyboard and the mouse costs cognitive energy, and breaks your flow. No need to use the mouse with Vim. There are countless plugins for Vim out there, enabling a more modern experience, similar to an IDE. You can use any shell command directly in Vim, expanding drastically its functionalities. Many command-line tools use some Vim keystrokes. It makes them easier to learn. Popular shells (like Bash or Zsh) have a "Vi" mode, allowing you to use some Vim keystrokes to edit your commands. Vim is sometimes the only option for editing files on remote server or docker containers. Is it true that Vim has a steep learning curve?

Despite its reputation, Vim is not hard to learn. It works differently than most editor or IDE out there, that's why many people find it difficult. If you accept that it requires some adaptation, you can learn the basics in a couple of hours.

Vim is a good example of a tool easy to learn but hard to master: you'll add new functionalities to your workflow overtime, improving your editing experience and your efficiency.

That's why this book takes a step-by-step approach.

Is this book about Vim, Neovim, or GVim?

This book is exclusively about Vim and Neovim running in a *nix shell (Unix-like shell like Zsh or Bash). This book is not about Vim running in a GUI, like GVim for example.

Do you use LLMs ("AI") to write this book?

No.

Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
item.description:
Shows running iOS simulators in the Finder sidebar so you can drag files in and out of them.

SimDrop ← Finder sidebar › Locations └── iPhone Duo/ ← one folder per *booted* simulator ├── Photos and Videos/ ← simulator Photos library └── Downloads/ ← Files app › On My iPhone › Downloads

Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal:

cp config.json ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/iPhone\ Duo/Downloads/ brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop

Or download SimDrop-macos.dmg from GitHub Releases. Requires macOS 15 or later. It is Developer ID signed and notarized. SimDrop isn't on the Mac App Store and can't be: the app and its helper must run unsandboxed to drive simctl and the simulators' folders.

Open SimDrop once. The window is only a settings page showing whether these two one-time approvals are done:

Background Service: allow SimDrop in System Settings › General › Login Items. Finder Extension: click Enable in the Finder banner (or turn on SimDrop under File Providers in System Settings).

After that it works silently in the background, including after a restart. The window can be closed.

After installing or upgrading, open SimDrop once. Replacing the app makes macOS drop its Finder extension (Finder then says the application can't be found) and stop the background helper. launchd refuses to start a helper whose recorded launch constraint came from the old copy (needs LWCR update, exit 78). Until the new version has been launched, no part of SimDrop can run to repair this. A Homebrew postflight_steps can't launch it either, because open fails inside the cask step sandbox. So the cask shows a caveat instead. Opening the app re-registers the extension and makes sure the helper answers with this build's version. If needed, it boots the stale launchd job out and registers the helper again.

Finder moves files when you drag within the same volume and copies only across volumes. File Provider locations live in ~/Library/CloudStorage on your startup disk, so dragging a file from the Desktop into SimDrop moves it. iCloud Drive and Google Drive behave the same way, and File Provider has no API to change this.

Hold ⌥ Option while dragging to copy instead. The other direction moves too: dragging a file out of a simulator's Downloads removes it from the simulator. Photos are read-only, so dragging them out always copies.

Making SimDrop copy by default like a USB drive would require it to be a separate volume (e.g. an FSKit file system), which would be a rewrite.

In icon view, photos show real previews without downloading them first. The extension provides downscaled thumbnails. Dropped images and videos are imported with simctl addmedia, so they show up in the Photos app. iOS renames them (e.g. IMG_0007.JPG), and Finder updates the name to match. Finder can't reject drops by file type, so anything that isn't an image or video is put in the same simulator's Downloads folder instead. Finder moves it there too. When that happens SimDrop posts a notification saying where the file went. (Known issue: clicking the notification doesn't open Finder yet.) The list mirrors the Photos library: it is read from Photos.sqlite, so photos deleted in the simulator (now in "Recently Deleted") disappear from Finder too. Deleting a photo in Finder moves it to the simulator's "Recently Deleted" (recoverable there for 30 days), with no confirmation dialog. If the Photos app is open in the simulator, SimDrop relaunches it so the change shows. Supports adding, opening, replacing and deleting files and folders. Deleting goes to the Mac's Trash, with no confirmation dialog. The file is removed from the simulator and lands in your Trash. Put Back restores it into the simulator. Renaming and moving items inside Downloads isn't supported yet, because item identifiers are path-based. Changes made inside the simulator appear in Finder within a few seconds. iOS simulators only. Real devices aren't supported: iOS doesn't expose the Files app storage over USB, and photos written to a real device's DCIM folder are not imported into its Photos library. Target Sandbox Role SimDrop (app) no Settings window. Registers the helper (SMAppService.agent) and the single File Provider domain. SimDropHelper (launchd agent) no Starts at login. Watches ~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Devices with FSEvents and tells Finder to refresh (signalEnumerator). Over XPC it runs xcrun simctl addmedia and moves deleted Downloads files to the Mac's Trash. It must be a plain tool in SimDrop.app/Contents/MacOS. As a separate .app bundle, signalEnumerator fails with "The application cannot be used right now". SimDropFileProvider (extension) yes NSFileProviderReplicatedExtension. Reads and writes simulator folders directly through a temporary-exception entitlement, and asks the helper to import photos and to trash files. Shared/ — Simulator discovery from device.plist (state == 3 means booted), plus path resolution.

Paths inside a simulator (~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Devices/<UDID>/):

Downloads: data/Containers/Shared/AppGroup/<UUID>/File Provider Storage/Downloads, where the group's metadata plist has MCMMetadataIdentifier = group.com.apple.FileProvider.LocalStorage. Photos: data/Media/DCIM/1xxAPPLE/. Library state comes from data/Media/PhotoData/Photos.sqlite (ZASSET, where ZTRASHEDSTATE = 0).

Implementation notes:

Change sync. The helper calls signalEnumerator(.workingSet). The working-set enumerator diffs against the last snapshot it handed out (stored in the extension's container) and reports removed items with didDeleteItems. Leaving an item out of the working set does not remove it from Finder. Deleting photos. The helper edits Photos.sqlite directly. It updates the same ZASSET columns an in-app delete changes (ZTRASHEDSTATE, ZTRASHEDREASON, ZTRASHEDDATE, ZMODIFICATIONDATE, Z_OPT), found by diffing the table before and after deleting in the Photos app. The tables have Core Data triggers calling NSCoreDataTriggerUpdateAffectedObjectValue, which only exists inside the Photos daemon, so the helper registers a no-op function with that name. The Photos app caches the library and only shows the change after a relaunch. This is unofficial: a future iOS schema change may break it, and the helper then reports an error instead of guessing. Thumbnails. Photos get previews through NSFileProviderThumbnailing. Finder only asks File Providers for thumbnails of media types, never for .app, .ipa or .zip (an app-install feature was tried and removed for now). Thumbnails are cached per content version, so bump Item.contentSchema after changing them. Re-imports. After the domain reconnects (e.g. following an upgrade), the system may call createItem for folders it already had, such as a simulator folder or its Downloads / Photos and Videos. These are adopted under their real identifiers. A rejected create stays pending forever, and the system ignores deletions of a pending item, so a shut-down simulator would never disappear. Folder types. Directories are always reported as public.folder, including bundles like .app. For uploads, the returned type must match the template, or the system keeps retrying the create and never uploads the children. Item versions. Item.metadataSchema is part of every metadata version. Bump it when capabilities change, or Finder keeps the cached ones (e.g. photos showing as "locked"). Trash. The domain keeps the default supportsSyncingTrash = YES, so Finder reparents trashed items to .trashContainer. modifyItem moves the real file to the Mac's Trash through the helper, and the next sync reports the item as deleted. The extension must serve .trashContainer (an empty folder). Otherwise the domain's .Trash becomes a stale handle and Finder fails with -36.

CI (.github/workflows/release.yml) runs when MARKETING_VERSION in project.yml changes on main. It generates the project with XcodeGen, then uses rxliuli/apple-release/dmg to archive, sign with Developer ID, build the DMG, notarize, staple and publish a GitHub Release. The release-macOS environment needs these secrets: APPLE_CERTIFICATE_DEVELOPERID_BASE64, APPLE_CERTIFICATE_DEVELOPERID_PASSWORD, APPLE_API_KEY, APPLE_API_KEY_ID, APPLE_API_ISSUER, and optionally TAP_GITHUB_TOKEN. When it is set, the release also bumps Casks/sim-drop.rb in rxliuli/homebrew-tap.

No provisioning profile is involved. The app group is Team-ID-prefixed (N2X78TUUFG.com.rxliuli.sim-drop, not group.…), which macOS accepts without one.

Requires XcodeGen.

xcodegen generate xcodebuild -project SimDrop.xcodeproj -scheme SimDrop -derivedDataPath build \ -allowProvisioningUpdates build # restart the extension and helper so they pick up the new build pkill -x SimDropFileProvider; launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.rxliuli.sim-drop.helper open build/Build/Products/Debug/SimDrop.app

App icon: the source is Design/icon-source.png (a full-bleed 1024 squircle with transparent corners). Regenerate the icon set with swift Design/make-icon.swift Design/icon-source.png SimDrop/Assets.xcassets/AppIcon.appiconset. The script scales the artwork to the 824pt macOS icon grid and adds a drop shadow.

Dev launch flags:

open SimDrop.app --args -reregisterHelper YES re-registers the launchd agent after its plist changes. open SimDrop.app --args -resetDomain YES removes the domain with all local state and re-adds it.

Don't remove the helper's launchd job on a plain uninstall (e.g. uninstall launchctl: in the cask). brew upgrade runs the old version's uninstall step before installing the new one, so the job disappears while the registration still says "enabled". The cask only does this on --zap.

Switching between a dev build and an installed release: only one copy should be registered. launchd records a launch constraint (LWCR) for the helper with the signing identity of whichever copy registered it. If that copy differs from the one now on disk (e.g. Apple Development vs Developer ID), launchd refuses to start the helper (last exit reason = OS_REASON_CODESIGNING). Quit the other copy, then run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.rxliuli.sim-drop.helper and launch the copy you want with --args -reregisterHelper YES. Duplicate extensions (pluginkit -m -v -D -i com.rxliuli.sim-drop.FileProvider) also hide SimDrop from System Settings › Login Items & Extensions.

item.description:
Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads.

Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"), and the skip button takes a few seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage.

Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time.

🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting.

Auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed.

Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time.

Incognito: see the Incognito section above.

 Ad detected → Capture timestamp → Reload page → Auto-seek to timestamp → Resume ↓ (if 3 reloads fail) Redirect to yout-ube.com (ad-free mirror, no looping)

Reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek.

yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay issue that the mirror has by default.

Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver)

Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage

Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL

Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes

Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops

 ✅ Zero ads — reloads until the ad is gone (usually 1-2 cycles) ✅ Timestamp preserved — never lose your place in the video ✅ Live streams — plain reload (no timestamp to preserve) ✅ Ad history database — every ad logged with advertiser, duration, skip text, video, and timestamp ✅ Export — JSON or CSV download of all collected ad data ✅ Popup viewer — click the extension icon to see stats, top advertisers, and full history ✅ No permissions abuse — only storage and tabs, only on YouTube domains Clone the repo: git clone https://github.com/antonpictures/youtube-punisher.git Open chrome://extensions Enable Developer mode (top right) Click Load unpacked → select the youtube-punisher folder Done — activates on all YouTube pages automatically. ✅ Tested

Safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. As a workaround, use the JS overlay + AppleScript watcher (yt-ad-watch.sh):

In Safari, enable: Safari → Settings → Advanced → Show Develop menu in menu bar In Safari (on a YouTube page), run ./yt-ad-watch.sh in Terminal When an ad appears, the watcher detects it via MutationObserver (event-driven in the page), reloads with &t=Xs, and the MutationObserver re-detects on the next page load

Note: This is best-effort. Chrome is fully reliable; Safari works but may need manual testing.

 Download the latest release from Releases Unzip and follow Option A steps 2–5

Every ad YouTube serves you is recorded:

Field What it captures Timestamp When the ad was detected Advertiser Company name from the ad overlay Video Title of the video you were watching Video time Your playback position before reload Ad duration Length of the ad Skip text "Skip Ad" button text (if available) Action Reloaded or skipped

Export as JSON or CSV from the popup. Data stays local — nothing is sent anywhere.

YouTube's ad system serves ads as part of the page load. When you reload, YouTube re-evaluates whether to serve an ad based on your session state. After 1-2 reloads, the ad slot is typically empty and the video plays directly. This is a client-side, zero-cost workaround — no filter lists, no network blocking, no detection by YouTube's anti-adblock system.

If millions of users did this, each reload = a full page load = server request. YouTube would see a spike in page loads but a drop in ad impressions. It's not a DDoS (no amplification, no botnet), but it's a passive protest: every reload is a vote that says "I will not watch your ad." The ad revenue model breaks when reloads are cheaper than ad views.

"Every reload is a vote: I will not watch your ad." — George Anton, creator

item.title: CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' indicted for wire fraud
item.description:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning
item.description:
Every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so. Where data is rare, that assumption decides the answer. This introduction explains where uncertainty comes from and how to judge when it needs to be faithful to be useful.

Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.

George E. P. Box

Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it. So most models carry some uncertainty, whether we chose it or not, and in many decisions it pays to take that uncertainty into account, as the examples in this post show.

In my experience, uncertainty in machine learning is a confusing topic to get into, so I wrote this introduction to give an intuitive overview. It is not comprehensive, but it should give you a good enough mental model to choose assumptions that make your uncertainty estimates useful for decision making, even though, as Box put it, the model itself will always be wrong.This post is based on a talk I gave at the University of Alicante. The slides are online. For a more thorough introduction, see Chapters 2 and 3 of my PhD thesis .

Generally speaking, uncertainty is incomplete knowledge, and probability is how we describe it: a distribution over the possible outcomes says how plausible each one is, given what we know.

It helps to separate two kinds of uncertainty:

Epistemic uncertainty comes from what we have not learned yet, such as the true relationship between inputs and outputs. More data can reduce it.Aleatoric uncertainty comes from what we cannot observe: the inputs do not determine the outcome, so more data of the same kind will not remove it.

The line between the two depends on what we measure. A coin flip follows classical mechanics. If we do not measure how the coin is thrown, the best we can say is 50/50, and the uncertainty is aleatoric. If we do measure it, physics tells us how it will land, and the uncertainty becomes epistemic: now we have to learn the physics, which takes data. Richer inputs can reduce aleatoric uncertainty, but they give the model more to learn, and whether that pays off depends on how much data and prior knowledge we have.Some inputs are out of reach. For example, weather is chaotic, so tiny differences, as small as the flap of a butterfly's wings, can grow into different weather a few weeks later. Since we cannot observe every butterfly, part of the uncertainty in a forecast stays aleatoric, however much we measure.

A prediction is not a decision. When we decide, we often weigh the possible outcomes by how likely they are and what they would cost us, including rare outcomes that could hurt us badly. A single number hides this picture. It also cannot tell us when to hand a case to a human or to collect more data before we decide. The examples below show where modelling uncertainty matters.

All of these need the uncertainty to be useful. To see when it is, it makes sense to look at where it comes from.

As a running example, we look at steering angle prediction. The input is the image from a car’s front camera, and the output $y$ is the steering angle. Such datasets can be recorded cheaply from human drivers. Take a car approaching a point where the road splits. In the left lane, drivers mostly go left. In the right lane, they mostly go right. In the middle lane, which points straight at the divider, about half go left and half go right.

The car’s position across the lanes is implicit in the camera image. To keep the figures simple, we use it directly as a one-dimensional input $x$ in the figures below.The rest of the image, such as where the road goes, matters just as much for the prediction. We implicitly assume that the model knows it, since it cannot be compressed into a simple one-dimensional variable that keeps the explanations easy to follow.

What we want to learn is the conditional distribution $p^*(y \mid x)$: for each position, how likely each steering angle is. As is common in statistical learning theory, we assume that the data come from a fixed joint distribution $p^*(x, y)$, and the recordings from human drivers are samples from it.

The ground truth $p^*(y \mid x)$ is just one of many possible conditional distributions.Strictly speaking, the truth is only defined where $p^*(x) > 0$. Many hypotheses agree with it on the road but differ off the road, where no data can tell them apart. We call each conditional distribution of $y$ given $x$ a hypothesis, and together they form a space. As we will see, learning amounts to searching a subset of this space.

That subset is the model, a family of hypotheses indexed by parameters $\theta$. A common choice for regression is a Gaussian whose mean is a neural network $f_\theta(x)$ and whose variance $\sigma^2$ is fixed:

\[p_\theta(y \mid x) = \mathcal{N}\big(y;\, f_\theta(x),\, \sigma^2\big).\]

The truth need not lie inside the model. For the lane split, it does not: a single Gaussian has one peak, but in the middle lane the truth has two.

Training picks the hypothesis that best explains the data. It minimizes the negative log-likelihood (NLL), the average of $-\log p_\theta(y_i \mid x_i)$ over the training examples. For the Gaussian with fixed variance, this is the familiar mean squared errorI walked through this connection, from the KL divergence to the mean squared error, in an earlier post.:

So a network trained with mean squared error already has an uncertainty model, even if nobody chose it on purpose.

How far is the trained model from the truth? The expected NLL splits into two terms:

\[\mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\text{NLL}] = \mathbb{E}_x\Big[\mathrm{KL}\big(p^* \,\|\, p_\theta\big)\Big] + \mathbb{E}_x\big[H(p^*)\big],\]

where both expectations are over the true data distribution. The first term is the KL divergence, which measures how far the model is from the truth and is zero only if they match. The second is the entropy of the truth, its aleatoric uncertainty, which does not depend on the model. Minimizing the NLL therefore moves the model toward the truth. But we never know the entropy of the truth, so the NLL alone cannot tell us how far away we still are.This is why we are usually blind to model misspecification: a low NLL does not tell us whether the truth lies inside the model. I will get back to this later. Moreover, even the KL divergence would not be enough, since it is an average over all inputs. In real driving data, lane splits are rare, so a model can be close to the truth on average and still steer into the divider. Knowing which inputs matter takes domain expertise, which is ultimately the modeller's responsibility.

Back in the middle lane, the single peak has a dangerous consequence. The mean squared error is minimized by the average steering angle, and the average of left and right is straight ahead, into the divider. No choice of parameters avoids this, because every hypothesis in the model has a single peak. In an earlier post, I looked at this example in more detail, and we studied it in a paper on misspecification, the case where the truth lies outside the model .

The fix is a model that contains the truth. For this example, a mixture of two Gaussians, whose weights, means and variances are all outputs of the network, is enough to contain the truth.

Understanding the problem well enough to make this choice is the modeller’s job. But a richer model is not free: it contains more hypotheses, so the data has to do more work to single out the right one.This is the familiar bias–variance tradeoff. For example, a fully connected network can represent everything a convolutional network can. Yet for images we use convolutional networks, because they leave out hypotheses that do not fit images and so need much less data. Their assumptions seem stronger than necessary, though: with enough data, vision transformers, which assume less, do better.

Since the mixture contains the truth, enough data brings it close, including in the middle lane. Only then is its spread the aleatoric uncertainty: with the given information, even a perfect model cannot say which lane a particular driver will take.As with the coin flip, what counts as aleatoric depends on what the input contains. If $x$ were random noise, it would carry no information, and the best fit would ignore it and learn the distribution of steering angles independent of the input, $p(y)$. A rear camera image is more deceptive. Steering changes slowly (it is strongly autocorrelated), so the view behind the car shows how the driver steered a moment ago, and repeating that is usually a good guess. The validation error decreases as expected during training, yet the model can never anticipate a turn, because the road ahead is not in the input. I discuss this gap between predicting and forecasting in an earlier post.

But in practice we do not know the truth, so we cannot check the fit like this. How do we know how much we still do not know?

So far, training gave us a single hypothesis. But with only 20 data points, many hypotheses explain the data about equally well, and by picking one of them, we ignore that the data cannot tell them apart. Bayesian inference instead keeps all of them.Bayesian inference is not the only way to capture epistemic uncertainty, but it is a principled one, and the one I know best.

Before seeing any data, we decide how plausible each hypothesis in the model is. This is the prior $p(\theta)$, a soft inductive bias. It captures what we know, or assume, before training, and everything the model does not know is measured relative to it.Choosing a prior can feel arbitrary, and often it is. Think of a CNN, which rules out hypotheses that do not suit images. A prior does not rule them out, but it makes them less plausible from the start. I discuss how the prior shapes what a model does not know in an earlier post. Data then shifts the weight to the hypotheses that explain it, giving rise to the posterior:

where $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ is the data. The likelihood, written $p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta)$ for short, measures how well hypothesis $\theta$ agrees with the data.

To predict, we average all hypotheses, each weighted by its posterior probability. This is the posterior predictive:

\[p(y \mid x, \mathcal{D}) = \int p_\theta(y \mid x) \, p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) \, \mathrm{d}\theta.\]

With more and more data, the posterior concentrates on a single hypothesis: the one in the model that is closest to the truth.Closest in KL divergence. This holds under regularity conditions, including that the prior puts enough weight near that hypothesis . If the model contains the truth, that hypothesis is the truth itself. If not, as in the sketch below, it is only the best the model has to offer.

This picture splits uncertainty into three sources, using the terms of Hüllermeier and Waegeman . What sets them apart is what reduces them:

Aleatoric: more data of the same kind, camera images paired with steering angles, does not help. Only more information in the input would, for example the driver’s route. Epistemic, what we have not learned, in two parts: Approximation: more data reduces it, since the posterior concentrates on the closest hypothesis.Model: more data does not fix it within the model. Only a different model does, one that is closer to the truth. Data can still guide the model selection, which is why this uncertainty is epistemic too.

The last point matters in practice. A misspecified model can still have a confident posterior: it is confident about the least wrong hypothesis it contains.

Both models above show more uncertainty where data is missing. That is approximation uncertainty, and both capture it. To also question the model itself, a full probabilistic treatment would weigh models too, but that is hard in practice. What we can do is compare a few candidate models. For this, Bayesian inference offers the evidence, $p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathcal{M}) = \int p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta) \, p(\theta \mid \mathcal{M}) \, \mathrm{d}\theta$, the probability of the data under model $\mathcal{M}$, averaged over its prior.The notation can be misleading, since it suggests that we treat the model as a random variable. We do not have to, so a semicolon, $p(\mathcal{D}; \mathcal{M})$, might be a preferable notation. Note also that $\mathcal{M}$ now includes the prior: the same hypotheses with a different prior form a different model. Here it clearly prefers the mixture.The evidence has a built-in Occam's razor : a more flexible model spreads its prior over more possible datasets, so it pays a price unless the data need that flexibility. Here, the two lanes do. But it only ranks the models we try, and if none of them contains the truth, it will not tell us.

Like the KL divergence earlier, the evidence is an average over all data. In real driving data, lane splits are rare, so their effect can vanish in the evidence, and the simpler model may even win. Domain knowledge would tell us otherwise. This is why choosing the model remains the modeller’s job, and comparing models is a tool for it, not a replacement.

So far, we have taken the prior as given. But the prior is part of the model. In theory, with enough data, its choice stops mattering, as long as it does not rule out the right hypotheses. In practice, we rarely have that much data, and a poor prior, like any poor inductive bias, can hurt a lot. I discussed this in more detail in earlier posts on uncertainty and on continual learning.

In short, the posterior is uncertain where the data and our assumptions leave room for disagreement. Low uncertainty therefore does not mean we have seen data there. Generalization works exactly this way: far from the data, the inductive bias makes the hypotheses agree. If the bias is good, the model is confident and right. If not, it is confident and wrong.

Sometimes we want a statistical guarantee, ideally one that does not depend on our modelling choices, since those can be arbitrarily wrong. Conformal prediction gives such a guarantee. Instead of a single prediction, it outputs a prediction set that contains the true output, say, 90% of the time. This is called 90% coverage. It wraps any trained model, and as long as the data are exchangeable, the guarantee holds no matter how wrong the model is .

Conformal prediction comes in many flavors. We look at the simplest and most common one, split conformal prediction. Its recipe has four steps:

Hold out a calibration set that the model was not trained on.Pick a score $s(x, y)$ that measures how wrong the model is on a pair $(x, y)$, for instance the absolute error $\lvert y - f(x) \rvert$.Take the 90% quantile $\hat q$ of the scores on the calibration set.Strictly, a slightly higher quantile, at level $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil / n$ for $n$ calibration examples and target coverage $1-\alpha$, to account for the finite calibration set.For a new input $x$, the prediction set contains every $y$ with $s(x, y) \le \hat q$.

If the calibration and test data are exchangeable, the set has at least 90% coverage. This holds on average over inputs, not for any particular input, such as one at the lane split.

But the guarantee does not say whether the sets are useful. For that, we want low scores in the histogram above, since a small $\hat q$ gives tight sets. A poor model has higher scores and gets wider sets, with the same coverage.

The guarantee only needs a calibration set. Useful sets also need the same modelling work as before. I wrote more about this in a recent post on conformal prediction.

So far, the goal was a faithful uncertainty: a predictive distribution close to the truth. But uncertainty is meant to be used, and decision theory says how. The model provides a belief $p(y \mid x)$. Whoever acts provides a loss $L(a, y)$, the cost of action $a$ if the outcome turns out to be $y$. We then pick the action with the lowest expected loss:

\[a^* = \arg\min_a \; \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y \mid x)}\big[L(a, y)\big].\]

In the lane split, the action is a steering angle. The belief says which angles drivers take: left or right, never straight. The loss says what we want. If our destination is to the left, steering left has a low loss, steering right a higher one, and steering into the divider is worst of all. Under the true belief, the decision follows the left lane. A belief with a single peak in the middle rules out neither lane and picks straight.

How faithful does the belief need to be? It depends on the decision.Since the belief is approximate anyway, we can fit it with the loss in mind, so that it is useful for the decision . In the rest of this section, we walk through two practical examples, visual quality inspection and holding reserve for wind power, where the answers differ.

Many factories use cameras to check every part that comes off the line. Mistakes are costly here, since a missed defect may reach a customer, lead to a recall or, in the worst case, put people at risk. To keep things simple, we consider a binary classifier in this section.In practice, a yes or no is rarely enough. We may also want to know where the defect is, its outline, which component it affects and why the model flagged it. It takes the camera image $x$ and outputs the probability $p(\text{defect} \mid x)$ that the part is defective. With stakes this high, should this probability not be faithful, or even come with a guarantee?

To answer this, we look at how the probability turns into a decision. We reject a part if $p = p(\text{defect} \mid x)$ is above a threshold. If we reject, we pay a cost $c_{FP}$ when the part is good, which happens with probability $1 - p$. If we ship, we pay a cost $c_{FN}$ when it is defective, which happens with probability $p$. Rejecting is cheaper on average when $c_{FP}\,(1 - p) < c_{FN}\,p$, that is, when

\[p(\text{defect} \mid x) > \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}.\]

What this derivation hides is that it takes $p$ at face value, so it assumes the model is calibrated: of all parts scored 0.1, about 10% should be defective. In this example, though, calibration matters less than it seems, for two reasons. First, calibrated against whom? Inspectors disagree on borderline parts, and since labels are expensive, each part is usually labeled by only one of them. So the labels can only tell us whether the model is calibrated against whoever labeled the data, and on borderline parts, another inspector would have labeled differently. Second, $c_{FN}$ includes recalls, lost customers and reputation, so it is rarely known. It is not even a single number, since a customer may never notice a faint scratch, while a deep crack can make the part fail. So the threshold is a guess anyway.

What about a guarantee, such as “at most 5% of defects escape”? The guarantee we got from conformal prediction earlier does not give this. It holds on average over all parts, and since defects are rare, it can be met while missing most of them. We need coverage for defects alone. Conformal prediction can give this too, if we set the threshold using defects only. Then at most a fraction $\alpha$ of defects, here 5%, score below it .

This guarantee has a price. Labeled defects are rare and expensive to collect, and we need many of them for a stable threshold. Worse, a defect is anything that is not normal. The guarantee holds only for defects that are exchangeable with the ones we collected, and the next one may look like none of them.Indeed, defects are so rare that practical solutions often teach the model with defect-free images only, an approach I worked on at Ethon (see here and here). Finally, the guarantee fixes the threshold, however many good parts it rejects.

If the model rejects too many good parts and we raise the threshold, we give up the guarantee and are back to costs we cannot measure.

So in this example, we need neither calibration nor a guarantee. Since $c_{FN}$ is unknown, an operator tunes the threshold by hand, and for that, only the order of the scores matters: they should grow with the severity of a flaw. Small scratches are rarely called defects and deep cracks almost always, and in between, inspectors disagree. A model calibrated against a large pool of inspectors would give such a score, but these labels are too expensive. Getting the order right without them is hard modelling work: we have to build the right inductive biases into the model, for instance during pre-training.

Wind power depends on the weather, so a grid operator never knows exactly how much will arrive. To cover a shortfall, meaning less wind power than planned, the operator keeps backup power on standby, called the reserve. Unlike inspecting parts, no person could forecast the shortfall by hand, so the model learns it from past data alone. It takes inputs $x$, such as the weather forecast and recent measurements, and outputs a distribution $p(\text{shortfall} \mid x)$ over the shortfall. If the shortfall exceeds the reserve, we have a shortage, and each missing unit costs $c_{\text{short}}$, and each unit of reserve that goes unused costs $c_{\text{idle}}$.In practice, $c_{\text{short}}$ is much larger. A shortage must be covered within minutes, by fast and expensive plants, by buying power at short notice or, in the worst case, by cutting off customers. Idle reserve only costs what it takes to keep a plant ready. Unlike $c_{FN}$ in visual inspection, both costs can be roughly estimated, for instance from market prices, so for the sake of argument, we take them as known.

The best reserve is the $\tau$-quantile of the predicted shortfall, with

\[\tau = \frac{c_{\text{short}}}{c_{\text{short}} + c_{\text{idle}}}.\]

The costs pick the quantile.Why the $\tau$-quantile? Say we hold a reserve $r$ and add one more unit. If the shortfall turns out larger than $r$, the unit is used and saves $c_{\text{short}}$. Otherwise, it sits idle and costs $c_{\text{idle}}$. So the unit pays off when $c_{\text{short}}\, P(\text{shortfall} > r) > c_{\text{idle}}\, P(\text{shortfall} \le r)$. As $r$ grows, the left side shrinks and the right side grows, so we add reserve until both are equal. With $P(\text{shortfall} > r) = 1 - P(\text{shortfall} \le r)$, this gives $P(\text{shortfall} \le r) = \tau$, which is the $\tau$-quantile. Since these costs change by the hour, so does $\tau$.

To see what this asks of the model, we again take a Gaussian model for simplicity. On most days, the forecast is roughly right, and the shortfall is small. But on rare days, the wind dies down unexpectedly, and the shortfall is large. So in the tail, the truth is not Gaussian. Since shortages are costly, $\tau$ is high, and the reserve sits far out in the tail of the predicted distribution, so the model has to get these rare, large shortfalls right.

If we plan for a shortage 1 in 10 times ($\tau = 90\%$), the two dots almost coincide, and the Gaussian works well. Now say we plan for 1 in 100 ($\tau = 99\%$). The Gaussian sets the reserve at the blue dot. But how often this reserve falls short is decided by the truth, and at this reserve, the orange curve lies well above 1 in 100. Shortages come more than twice as often as planned. Unlike in visual inspection, the probabilities are used at face value here,Why not adjust the reserve by hand, as the operator did with the threshold? In inspection, there is one threshold to tune. Here, $\tau$ changes by the hour, so every quantile would need tuning, and shortages are too rare to notice when one is off. and since $\tau$ changes by the hour, the whole distribution must be faithful, tail included.

In a year of daily data, a 1-in-100 shortfall shows up only a few times, and anything rarer than once a year not at all. So where we need the uncertainty most, in the tail, we have the least data, and the assumptions built into the model decide the answer. We have to choose them from what we know about wind and weather.

Every model in this post made an assumption about uncertainty, whether we chose it or not. Making it faithful took real work: a likelihood that can represent the truth, enough data to find it, and inductive biases that hold up where the data runs out.

That work is not always needed. Our own uncertainty is not faithful either. We humans misjudge probabilities in well-known ways , yet we handle most everyday tasks just fine. In this post, too, we saw tasks where uncertainty did not have to be faithful, and others where it counted. So before investing in faithful uncertainty, ask what you gain from it. And even when it does not have to be faithful, I believe it helps to know what faithful would mean. Then we know what our uncertainty gets wrong and can judge whether that matters for the decision.

Feedback is welcome. If you think this introduction misses an important aspect, or you know other examples where making uncertainty useful matters, please leave a comment below.
